title: 22. Interview: Service Discovery
summary: Interview Q&A for Service Discovery — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Service Discovery interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Why is hardcoding IP addresses or DNS hostnames insufficient for a microservices system?
**Answer:** Hardcoded addresses break the moment any instance is added, removed, or relocated — which in a microservices system with autoscaling and rolling deploys happens every few minutes. DNS improves on this by giving a stable name to a changing set of IPs, but standard DNS has three problems: TTL caching means clients hold stale records for the TTL duration (often 60s or more, during which they will keep sending traffic to dead instances); DNS does not carry health information, so a record may list an instance that is alive-but-not-ready; and DNS lookups add latency to every call if not cached aggressively. Service discovery solves all three: the registry is updated within seconds of an instance change, health checks ensure only ready instances are listed, and clients cache the registry with short TTLs (5–10s) so they get fresh data without per-call latency. Netflix's Eureka was built specifically because DNS did not meet their agility needs in 2012 — their fleet of microservices was changing too fast for DNS TTLs to keep up, and they needed health-aware routing that DNS could not provide.
**Visual:**
```
hardcoded:  caller -> 10.0.1.5:8080  (instance moved? call fails)
DNS:        caller -> billing.svc -> [10.0.1.5, 10.0.1.6] (stale for TTL=60s, no health)
registry:   caller -> resolve("billing") -> [healthy instances] (5s cache, health-aware)
```

### Q2. Contrast client-side and server-side discovery. When is each preferable?
**Answer:** In client-side discovery (Eureka + Ribbon, Consul + internal LB), the client queries the registry directly, gets the full instance list, and chooses one itself — giving it full control over load-balancing policy. In server-side discovery (Kubernetes Services, AWS ALB, Envoy as a front proxy), the client calls a stable virtual address and a router picks an instance. Client-side is preferable when you need fine-grained routing policy: zone-affinity (prefer instances in the same AZ to reduce cross-AZ latency and cost), latency-aware routing (pick the instance with the lowest p99 over the last minute), weighted canary routing (5% to v2, 95% to v1), or sticky sessions. Netflix uses client-side because all of these matter at their scale. Server-side is preferable when you want simplicity and language-agnostic behavior: any client (curl, browser, any language) can call a Service IP without a registry client library, and the platform handles the routing. Most Kubernetes users land on server-side for the platform integration, then add a service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) when they need client-side policies — the sidecar gives them client-side power with server-side simplicity for the application.
**Visual:**
```
client-side:  caller --query--> registry --[list]--> caller --pick--> instance
              (caller has LB logic; flexible; needs registry client lib per language)
server-side:  caller --call--> virtual IP --router picks--> instance
              (caller is dumb; simple; LB policy limited to router's capabilities)
mesh:         caller --localhost--> sidecar --query--> registry --pick--> instance
              (app sees server-side simplicity; sidecar has client-side power)
```

### Q3. Why does Netflix Eureka choose AP (availability + partition tolerance) over CP (consistency)?
**Answer:** Eureka is AP because the cost of being unavailable — refusing to answer resolve queries during a partition — is worse than the cost of being stale. If a registry node refuses to answer, every caller that depends on it cannot make service calls, which means the entire system goes down even though the actual services are healthy. By answering with stale data, Eureka lets calls proceed; if the stale data points to a dead instance, the caller's retry and circuit breaker handle it. The stale window is bounded by the heartbeat TTL (90s in Eureka's default), so the worst case is "callers try a dead instance, get a connection error, retry a different instance from the same list, succeed." This is the right trade-off for discovery because the system already has to handle transient failures at the call layer — adding "the registry might be briefly stale" is just one more transient failure to retry through. CP systems (etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul in CP mode) use Raft or Paxos, which means a partition makes the minority side refuse reads to preserve linearizability — fine for configuration or leadership election, but a bad default for pure discovery. The CAP choice should match the workload: AP for discovery, CP for coordination.
**Visual:**
```
AP (Eureka):       partition -> serve stale list (callers retry dead instances)
                   worst case: 90s of extra retries, no system outage
CP (etcd/ZK):      partition -> minority refuses reads (callers cannot resolve)
                   worst case: system outage because callers cannot find services
rule:              AP for discovery (callers already retry); CP for coordination (writes)
```

### Q4. What is the difference between a liveness probe and a readiness probe, and why does Kubernetes have both?
**Answer:** A liveness probe answers "is this process alive and not deadlocked?" — if it fails, Kubernetes restarts the pod, on the assumption that the process is in a bad state it cannot recover from (e.g., a deadlock, an infinite loop, a memory leak that has not yet OOMed). A readiness probe answers "is this process ready to serve traffic?" — if it fails, Kubernetes removes the pod from the Service's endpoint list, so no new traffic is sent to it, but the pod is not restarted. The distinction matters because a pod can be alive but not ready: during startup, the pod may need to load a large cache before it can serve (liveness = OK, readiness = false); during a downstream outage, the pod may be unable to serve requests because its DB connection pool is exhausted (liveness = OK if the probe is local-only, readiness = false); during a GC pause, the pod may be briefly unresponsive (liveness might fail, triggering a restart — which is sometimes what you want). The standard pattern is to make liveness cheap and local (e.g., a TCP check or a /healthz that returns 200 if the process is up) and readiness more thorough (e.g., a /readyz that checks DB connectivity, cache warmth, and downstream availability). Confusing the two — using a thorough check as liveness, so a downstream outage causes your pods to be killed — is a classic Kubernetes anti-pattern that causes cascading restarts.
**Visual:**
```
liveness:    "process alive?"  -> fail = restart pod
readiness:   "ready to serve?" -> fail = remove from Service endpoints (no restart)
startup:     liveness=OK, readiness=false (loading cache, no traffic yet)
DB outage:   liveness=OK (probe is local), readiness=false (cannot serve)
mistake:     thorough check as liveness -> downstream outage -> pod restarts -> worse
```

### Q5. How does service discovery work in Kubernetes, and what role does kube-dns play?
**Answer:** Kubernetes provides discovery through three layers that compose cleanly. First, every Service has a stable virtual IP (the ClusterIP) that does not change for the Service's lifetime, and a stable DNS name (`billing-service.namespace.svc.cluster.local`) that resolves to that IP via kube-dns (CoreDNS in modern clusters). Second, kube-proxy on every node programs iptables (or IPVS) rules that rewrite traffic destined for the ClusterIP to one of the pod IPs behind the Service, using round-robin or random selection. Third, the Service's endpoint list is maintained by the Kubernetes controller, which watches pod labels and readiness probes and updates the Endpoints object (or EndpointSlice) whenever pods are added, removed, or change readiness. So a caller that does `curl http://billing-service:8080/charge` is using all three layers: DNS resolves to ClusterIP, kube-proxy routes to a pod IP, and the pod IP list is kept current by the controller based on readiness. This is server-side discovery — the caller knows nothing about pods or endpoints, only the service name. The trade-off is that the load balancing is simple (iptables random or round-robin), so if you need zone-affinity, latency-aware routing, or canary weights, you add a service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) which intercepts traffic at the sidecar and applies those policies.
**Visual:**
```
caller -> curl http://billing-service:8080
  1. kube-dns resolves billing-service -> ClusterIP 10.96.0.5
  2. kube-proxy iptables: 10.96.0.5 -> [pod1:8080, pod2:8080] (round-robin)
  3. controller maintains pod list based on readiness probes
caller sees: just a hostname; no knowledge of pods, IPs, or health
```

### Q6. What is a service mesh, and how does it change the discovery story?
**Answer:** A service mesh (Istio, Linkerd, Consul Connect) inserts a sidecar proxy (Envoy for Istio, a Rust proxy for Linkerd) next to every service instance, and routes all inter-service traffic through these sidecars. From the application's perspective, calling another service is just a localhost call to the sidecar, which then handles discovery, load balancing, retries, circuit breaking, mTLS, and observability — the application code is unaware of any of it. The mesh changes the discovery story in three ways. First, it gives you client-side power with server-side simplicity: the sidecar queries the registry, applies sophisticated routing (zone-affinity, latency-aware, canary weights), and the application just calls `localhost:8080`. Second, it unifies policy across languages: a polyglot system with Java, Go, Python, and Node services gets the same retry, circuit-breaker, and mTLS behavior without each language re-implementing it. Third, it shifts observability: the sidecar emits spans, metrics, and access logs uniformly, so you get distributed tracing "for free." The cost is resource overhead (each pod runs an extra proxy, ~50–100MB RAM and some CPU) and operational complexity (the mesh control plane is itself a distributed system to operate). Netflix's internal mesh (Hystrix + Ribbon + Eureka) was the prototype; the open-source wave (Istio, Linkerd) generalized it. Most teams adopt a mesh when they have >50 services and the per-language duplication of resilience logic becomes painful.
**Visual:**
```
without mesh:  app --call--> registry --[instances]--> app picks one --call--> instance
                     (each language re-implements LB, retry, breaker, mTLS)
with mesh:     app --localhost--> sidecar --registry--> sidecar --pick--> instance sidecar -> app
                     (sidecar handles all of it; app code is unchanged across languages)
```

### Q7. How does service discovery interact with autoscaling and rolling deploys?
**Answer:** Autoscaling and rolling deploys are the events that make discovery necessary, and the registry must keep up with them in real time. During an autoscale event, the cluster controller adds N new pods; each pod registers with the registry (or, in Kubernetes, is added to the Service's Endpoints) once its readiness probe passes, and within seconds callers start routing traffic to the new pods. During a rolling deploy, the cluster replaces old-version pods with new-version pods one at a time (or in batches), and the registry must remove each old pod before its replacement is fully ready, to avoid both dropping traffic (old removed before new ready) and serving mixed versions for too long (old kept after new ready). Kubernetes handles this with `maxUnavailable` and `maxSurge` parameters — `maxSurge=1, maxUnavailable=0` means a new pod is created before any old pod is removed, so capacity is never reduced. Service meshes add finer control: Istio's weighted routing can send 5% of traffic to the new version, monitor error rate, and ramp to 100% only if healthy (a canary deploy). The failure mode to avoid is the "thundering herd": a registry that takes 60s to register a new pod means autoscaling is too slow to handle a traffic burst, and the system overloads before new capacity is usable. The fix is fast registration (Kubernetes adds to Endpoints within 5s of readiness passing) and pre-warming (HPC patterns where new pods are added to the registry but receive no traffic until they have served a few warmup requests).
**Visual:**
```
autoscale:  HPA -> add pods -> readiness passes -> added to Endpoints (5s) -> traffic flows
rolling:    maxSurge=1, maxUnavailable=0 -> new pod ready BEFORE old removed
canary:     Istio weighted: 5% -> v2, 95% -> v1; ramp if error rate < threshold
failure:    registry slow to register -> new capacity unusable -> overload during burst
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You are running Netflix-style microservices on Eureka. A network partition splits the cluster; the registry nodes on the minority side cannot reach the majority. What happens to service calls?
**Answer:** Because Eureka is AP, the minority-side registry nodes continue serving their cached instance lists rather than refusing queries — this is the deliberate trade-off. Callers on the minority side resolve service names against the stale list and attempt calls; some calls succeed (instances that are still reachable), some fail (instances on the majority side, now unreachable). Each caller's retry and circuit breaker handle the failures: after a few failed calls to a now-unreachable instance, the circuit opens and the caller stops trying it, eventually failing fast or falling back. The system degrades rather than collapses — user-facing requests that depend only on minority-side services succeed, requests that need majority-side services fail with a fallback (cached data, degraded feature). When the partition heals, Eureka nodes resynchronize, the stale instances are corrected, and circuit breakers close as calls succeed again. The key engineering lesson is that AP discovery works only because the call layer is also designed for partial failure — without retries, circuit breakers, and fallbacks, the stale registry data would cause cascading failures. This is why Netflix built Hystrix alongside Eureka: discovery and resilience are co-designs, not independent components.
**Visual:**
```
partition:  majority side (5 nodes) | minority side (3 nodes)
Eureka AP:  minority serves stale instance list (does not refuse)
callers:    try stale endpoints -> some succeed, some fail
            retry -> circuit breaker opens for dead instances -> fallback
heal:       nodes resync, instances corrected, breakers close
lesson:     AP discovery works ONLY if call layer has retries + breakers + fallbacks
```

### Q2. You migrate from Eureka to Kubernetes Services. The dev team complains that "circuit breakers don't work anymore — we still see traffic going to dead pods." Diagnose.
**Answer:** The diagnosis is that the team is conflating discovery with circuit breaking — they were both bundled in Hystrix + Ribbon, and the Kubernetes migration only replaced discovery, not the breaker. In Eureka, Ribbon's client-side load balancer was also the circuit breaker: when an instance failed, Ribbon opened the breaker for that instance and stopped sending it traffic. In Kubernetes, kube-proxy routes traffic to whatever is in the Endpoints list, and the Endpoints list is updated by the readiness probe — but readiness is updated at most every few seconds, and a pod can be in the Endpoints list but failing (e.g., intermittent 500s, slow responses) without its readiness probe failing. The fix is to add a circuit breaker at the call layer, separate from the platform's discovery. Options: use Resilience4j in the application code (explicit, per-service), adopt a service mesh like Istio or Linkerd (the sidecar does outlier detection — it tracks per-instance error rates and ejects failing instances from its load-balancing pool, which is the mesh equivalent of a circuit breaker), or use a client library that does both discovery and breaking (Spring Cloud LoadBalancer + Resilience4j). The deeper lesson is that Kubernetes gives you discovery and health-checking for free, but resilience (breaking, fallbacks, retries) is still your job — and a service mesh is the cleanest way to provide it without per-language re-implementation.
**Visual:**
```
Eureka:    Ribbon = discovery + circuit breaker (bundled)
K8s:       kube-proxy = discovery only (no breaker)
           Endpoints updated by readiness -> slow, coarse
dead pod still in Endpoints? -> kube-proxy sends traffic -> 500s
fix:  Resilience4j per service, OR Istio outlier detection (per-instance breaker in sidecar)
lesson: K8s gives discovery; resilience is still your job (or your mesh's)
```

### Q3. HashiCorp Consul is your registry. A service instance crashes without deregistering. How does Consul eventually remove it?
**Answer:** Consul uses two complementary mechanisms to remove crashed instances. First, **passive health checking via TTL**: each registered service is expected to call Consul's TTL check endpoint every N seconds (e.g., 30s); if Consul does not receive the TTL call within the configured window plus a grace period, it marks the service critical. The crashed process stops sending TTLs, so after the TTL expires (typically 30–90s), Consul marks it critical and removes it from DNS and API queries. Second, **active health checks**: Consul can be configured to poll an HTTP, TCP, or script health check on each instance at a regular interval; if the check fails, the instance is marked critical regardless of TTL. Active checks catch the "TTL is being sent but the service cannot actually serve" case — e.g., a process that is alive enough to send TTLs but whose HTTP server is hung. The combination is the same pattern Eureka and Kubernetes use: passive (heartbeat) catches process death, active (probe) catches process zombie. The configuration choice is the TTL/probe interval: too short and you generate excessive load and false negatives during transient slowness; too long and dead instances linger in the registry. Consul's defaults are 10s interval with 4 failures before critical (~40s), which is a reasonable starting point. The architect's job is to set these per service based on its SLO — a latency-critical service may want 5s intervals, while a batch service may be fine with 60s.
**Visual:**
```
crash (no deregister):
  1. process dies -> stops sending TTL checks
  2. Consul TTL window (30-90s) expires -> mark critical -> remove from DNS/API
  3. active HTTP check also fails -> confirms critical (catches zombie case)
both:  passive (TTL) catches death; active (probe) catches zombie
tuning: 5s for latency-critical, 60s for batch; default 10s/4 failures is reasonable
```

### Q4. You have a service that needs to call billing-service, but every call routes to the same instance while the other 4 sit idle. Diagnose.
**Answer:** The diagnosis is a load-balancing distribution problem — the client is not varying its instance selection across calls. The most likely causes, in order. First, **DNS caching**: if the client is using DNS-based discovery (e.g., `billing-service.svc.cluster.local`) and caching the resolved IP for a long TTL (some JVMs cache for 60s by default, and `networkaddress.cache.ttl` can be set to `-1` for "forever"), every call in the cache window goes to the same IP. Fix by setting a short DNS TTL (5s) or using the registry's API directly. Second, **client-side LB with sticky selection**: if the client uses Ribbon or a similar LB and the load-balancing rule is `BestAvailable` or `ZoneAffinity`, it may stick to one instance that is "good enough." Fix by using `RoundRobin` or `WeightedResponseTime`. Third, **HTTP keep-alive**: if the client reuses a single HTTP connection to one instance (connection pooling), every call goes to that instance until the connection is closed. Fix by either disabling keep-alive (costs latency) or using client-side LB that selects per-request, not per-connection. Fourth, **kube-proxy in iptables mode with `sessionAffinity: ClientIP`**: if the Service has session affinity enabled, all calls from the same client IP go to the same pod. Fix by disabling session affinity unless you specifically need it (sticky sessions). The diagnostic is to log which instance IP each call hits; if all calls hit the same IP, work through the four causes above.
**Visual:**
```
all calls -> instance1, others idle:
  1. DNS cache (JVM caches 60s or forever) -> fix: short TTL
  2. sticky LB rule (BestAvailable, ZoneAffinity) -> fix: RoundRobin
  3. HTTP keep-alive reuses one connection -> fix: per-request LB
  4. kube-proxy sessionAffinity=ClientIP -> fix: disable unless needed
diagnose: log instance IP per call; if same IP -> walk these 4 causes
```

### Q5. You run 1000 microservices in Kubernetes. DNS resolution latency is showing up as a significant fraction of p99 latency. How do you optimize?
**Answer:** DNS resolution on every call is wasteful — most services call the same handful of downstream services repeatedly, so the resolution can be cached. The optimizations, in order of impact. First, **enable DNS caching in the application**: most HTTP clients (OkHttp, Go's net/http, Python's requests) cache DNS results per-process for a configurable TTL; set this to 5–30s for service calls. The JVM's `networkaddress.cache.ttl=10` is a common setting. Second, **use the cluster's DNS cache efficiently**: CoreDNS (kube-dns) is the resolver; ensure it has enough replicas and CPU, and consider enabling the NodeLocal DNSCache (a DaemonSet that caches DNS on every node, eliminating the cross-node hop to CoreDNS). Google's GKE and AWS's EKS both ship NodeLocal DNSCache as a recommended add-on because it cuts DNS latency from ~5ms to ~0.1ms. Third, **resolve once and reuse**: a service that starts up and resolves its downstream dependencies once (with a refresh every 30s in the background) pays the DNS cost once per 30s, not once per call. Fourth, **consider replacing DNS with the registry API**: in client-side discovery, the registry client caches the instance list and refreshes it asynchronously, so calls never block on DNS. Fifth, **for the hottest paths, use IP-based discovery**: a service mesh like Istio uses the registry directly, bypassing DNS for inter-service calls — the sidecar has the instance list in memory and routes based on the service name, with no DNS lookup at call time. The combined effect can take DNS from a 5ms p99 contributor to a 0.1ms contributor.
**Visual:**
```
no cache:     every call -> DNS lookup (5ms p99) -> significant at p99
fixes (impact order):
  1. app-level DNS cache (JVM ttl=10, OkHttp cache) -> 0ms after first call
  2. NodeLocal DNSCache DaemonSet -> 5ms -> 0.1ms (no cross-node hop)
  3. resolve once, refresh every 30s in background
  4. registry API client (no DNS per call)
  5. service mesh (sidecar has instance list, no DNS for inter-svc)
```

### Q6. A new pod starts up and is added to the Service's Endpoints, but it immediately receives traffic and returns 500s because its in-memory cache is still loading. How do you prevent this?
**Answer:** The diagnosis is that the readiness probe passed before the pod was actually ready to serve, because the probe checked only "is the process up" rather than "is the cache loaded." The fix is to make the readiness probe check the actual readiness condition. For a pod that needs a warmed cache, the readiness endpoint should return 503 until the cache is loaded, then 200 once it is. The pod's startup code loads the cache (either eagerly, before starting the HTTP server, or in a background task with a `cache_ready` flag), and the `/readyz` endpoint checks that flag. Kubernetes then keeps the pod out of the Endpoints list until `/readyz` returns 200, so no traffic is sent during the loading window. A second refinement is the **startup probe** (Kubernetes 1.18+): a separate probe that gates liveness checks during startup, so a slow-to-start pod is not killed by the liveness probe before it has finished initializing. A third refinement is **pre-warming**: the pod can be added to the Endpoints but receive a small trickle of traffic (e.g., 1 req/s) for a warmup period before being fully eligible — this is what service meshes like Istio enable with weighted routing during a "warmup" phase. The deeper lesson is that readiness is a semantic condition, not a network condition — the readiness probe must reflect what "ready" means for this specific service, which is usually "I have loaded my cache and my downstream dependencies are reachable," not just "my HTTP server is listening."
**Visual:**
```
WRONG:  readiness = TCP check on port 8080 -> returns OK immediately -> 500s during cache load
RIGHT:  /readyz returns 503 until cache_ready=true, then 200
        pod stays out of Endpoints until /readyz=200 -> no traffic during load
PLUS:   startup probe (slow init) -> gates liveness so pod isn't killed during init
PLUS:   Istio warmup -> 1 req/s trickle for 60s, then full traffic
```

### Q7. You are designing a hybrid system: some services run on Kubernetes, some on EC2 VMs, some on Lambda. How do you implement service discovery across all three?
**Answer:** The hybrid case requires a registry that is not tied to one platform, and the standard answer is HashiCorp Consul or an equivalent cross-platform registry. Each platform's services register with Consul: Kubernetes services register via a Consul agent DaemonSet (or the Consul Connect mesh), EC2 services register via a Consul agent on the host, Lambda functions register via a registration step on cold start (or are represented as a stable API Gateway endpoint that Consul resolves to). All services then resolve each other through Consul's API or DNS, regardless of where they run. The complications are three. First, **Lambda's lifecycle**: functions do not have long-running processes, so they cannot heartbeat; represent them as a stable endpoint (the API Gateway URL or the function URL) that Consul points to, and let Lambda's own scaling handle capacity. Second, **health checking across platforms**: Kubernetes has its own probes, EC2 has CloudWatch or agent checks, Lambda has no health check (it is invoked on demand); normalize by having each platform report to Consul in its own way and treating "Lambda is always healthy if the function exists" as the simplification. Third, **latency**: cross-platform calls may go over the internet or VPC peering, which is slower than intra-cluster calls; the registry can carry metadata (region, AZ, platform) so callers can prefer same-platform or same-region instances for latency. The alternative to Consul is to expose every platform through an API gateway and use the gateway as the discovery layer — simpler, but loses the per-instance granularity. The architect's choice depends on whether per-instance routing matters; for most hybrid systems, gateway-level discovery is sufficient and far simpler.
**Visual:**
```
K8s svc --Consul agent--> Consul <--Consul agent-- EC2 svc
                                 ^
                                 +-- API Gateway URL <-- Lambda fn
all resolve via Consul DNS:  billing.service.consul -> [k8s:8080, ec2:8081, lambda-url]
metadata: region, az, platform -> callers prefer same-region for latency
or simpler: every platform behind an API gateway, gateway is the discovery layer
```
